title: Entropy
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 7
summary:
Entropy turns the second law from a set of statements into a **property you can compute**. It starts from the **Clausius inequality**, $\oint \delta Q/T \le 0$: integrated around any cycle, the heat-over-temperature is zero for a reversible cycle and negative otherwise. The reversible case lets us define entropy by $dS = (\delta Q/T)_{int,rev}$. Because $S$ is a property, $\Delta S$ between two states is fixed by the endpoints alone — you may compute it along any convenient reversible path, even if the real process was messy.

The headline result is the **increase-of-entropy principle**: the entropy of an *isolated* system can only increase or, at best (reversible), stay the same. For any system plus its surroundings, $S_{gen} = \Delta S_{total} \ge 0$. Entropy generation $S_{gen}$ measures irreversibility: zero for a reversible process, positive for a real one, never negative. A process with $S_{gen} < 0$ is impossible.

To actually evaluate $\Delta s$ we use the **$T\,ds$ (Gibbs) relations**, $T\,ds = du + P\,dv$ and $T\,ds = dh - v\,dP$. Integrating them for an **ideal gas** with constant specific heats gives two interchangeable forms: $\Delta s = c_v\ln(T_2/T_1) + R\ln(v_2/v_1)$ and $\Delta s = c_p\ln(T_2/T_1) - R\ln(P_2/P_1)$ — pick whichever matches the variables you're given. These are the **approximate** treatment; when the temperature change is large and $c_p$ varies a lot, use the **exact** treatment with the tabulated function $s^\circ(T) = \int_0^T c_p\,dT/T$: $\Delta s = s_2^\circ - s_1^\circ - R\ln(P_2/P_1)$, reading $s^\circ$ straight from the ideal-gas table (A-17 for air). For an **incompressible** solid or liquid it simplifies to $\Delta s = c\ln(T_2/T_1)$.

A process that is both adiabatic and reversible has $\Delta s = 0$ — it is **isentropic**, the ideal model for turbines, compressors, pumps and nozzles. For an ideal gas with constant specific heats, isentropic states are linked by $T_2/T_1 = (P_2/P_1)^{(k-1)/k} = (v_1/v_2)^{k-1}$ and $Pv^k = \text{const}$. For a **large** temperature change, or when you're given a **volume ratio** (engine compression ratios), the accurate route is the tabulated **relative pressure** $P_r$ and **relative specific volume** $v_r$ (functions of $T$ only): $(P_2/P_1)_s = P_{r2}/P_{r1}$ and $(v_2/v_1)_s = v_{r2}/v_{r1}$. Real devices fall short of the isentropic ideal, and the gap is quantified by **isentropic efficiency**: for a turbine $\eta_T = (h_1 - h_2)/(h_1 - h_{2s})$ (actual drop ÷ ideal drop); for a compressor the ratio inverts; for a nozzle $\eta_N = V_{2a}^2/V_{2s}^2$ compares actual and ideal exit kinetic energy.

For **steady-flow** devices the reversible work is $w_{rev} = -\int v\,dP$ (plus KE/PE) — note it depends on $v\,dP$, not the closed-system $P\,dv$. Since the work scales with specific volume, compressing an ideal gas costs least along an **isothermal** path and most along an **isentropic** one; real compressors approach the cheap isothermal limit using **multistage compression with intercooling**, whose work is minimized when the pressure ratio is equal across each stage (for two stages, $P_x = \sqrt{P_1 P_2}$).

Finally, the **entropy balance**, $S_{in} - S_{out} + S_{gen} = \Delta S_{system}$, with entropy transported by heat as $\sum Q_k/T_k$, ties it all together — the second-law counterpart of the energy balance, and the tool for finding $S_{gen}$ in any device. The workflow: pick the right $\Delta s$ form for the substance and given data; for ideal devices set $\Delta s = 0$; for real ones, use isentropic efficiency or the entropy balance.

equations.name: Clausius inequality & entropy definition
equations.useWhen: Establishing entropy as a property and computing $\Delta S$ for heat exchange at a known temperature (e.g. a reservoir at constant $T$).
equations.note: Equality holds for reversible cycles; "<" for irreversible ones.

equations.name: Increase-of-entropy principle
equations.useWhen: Judging feasibility and measuring irreversibility. Compute the total entropy change of system + surroundings; it must be $\ge 0$.
equations.note: Entropy is NOT conserved — it is generated by irreversibility.

equations.name: T ds (Gibbs) relations
equations.latex: T\,ds = du + P\,dv, \qquad T\,ds = dh - v\,dP
equations.useWhen: The starting point for deriving every $\Delta s$ formula. Use the $du$ form with volume data, the $dh$ form with pressure data.
equations.note: These connect entropy to measurable properties; integrate them for each substance type.

equations.name: Entropy change of an ideal gas
equations.useWhen: An ideal-gas process where the temperature change is modest (a few hundred K) so $c_v, c_p$ can be treated as constant. Choose the $(T,v)$ or $(T,P)$ form to match the data. Temperatures in K.
equations.note: This is the **approximate** (constant-specific-heat) treatment. When $\Delta T$ is large and specific heats vary a lot, switch to the exact $s^\circ$ method below.

equations.name: Ideal-gas Δs — variable specific heats (exact, s°)
rearrangements: \bar s_2 - \bar s_1 = \bar s_2^\circ - \bar s_1^\circ - R_u\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}\ (\text{per kmol})
equations.useWhen: Large temperature swings, where constant-$c_p$ would be inaccurate. Read $s^\circ(T_1)$ and $s^\circ(T_2)$ straight from the ideal-gas table (A-17 for air) and add the pressure term.
equations.note: $s^\circ$ captures only the **temperature** part of entropy (it's a function of $T$ alone); the $-R\ln(P_2/P_1)$ term adds the pressure dependence. Unlike $u$ and $h$, an ideal gas's entropy depends on $P$ too, so it can't be tabulated against $T$ alone.

equations.name: Entropy change of an incompressible substance
equations.useWhen: Heating or cooling a solid or liquid. No pressure term — volume barely changes. Temperatures in K.
equations.note: Isentropic ($\Delta s = 0$) for an incompressible substance means $T_2 = T_1$.

equations.name: Isentropic ideal-gas relations
equations.useWhen: An ideal gas undergoes a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) process — the ideal model for turbines, compressors, nozzles — **when $\Delta T$ is modest** so constant $k$ is acceptable. Find the ideal exit state.
equations.note: Constant specific heats, $k = c_p/c_v$. Temperatures and pressures absolute. For large $\Delta T$, use the relative-pressure/volume method below instead.

equations.name: Isentropic ideal gas — relative pressure & volume (P_r, v_r)
equations.useWhen: An **isentropic** ideal-gas process with a **large** temperature change, where constant-$k$ relations lose accuracy. Also the natural tool for **volume-ratio** problems (e.g. an engine compression ratio $V_1/V_2$).
equations.note: $P_r$ (relative pressure) and $v_r$ (relative specific volume) are dimensionless, tabulated functions of **temperature only** (Table A-17). Recipe: read $P_{r1}$ (or $v_{r1}$) at $T_1$, scale by the pressure (or volume) ratio, then read $T_2$ off the table at the new $P_r$ (or $v_r$).

equations.name: Isentropic efficiency (turbine, compressor, nozzle)
equations.latex: \eta_T = \frac{h_1 - h_2}{h_1 - h_{2s}}, \quad \eta_C = \frac{h_{2s} - h_1}{h_2 - h_1}, \quad \eta_N = \frac{V_{2a}^2}{V_{2s}^2} = \frac{h_1 - h_{2a}}{h_1 - h_{2s}}
equations.useWhen: Relating a real adiabatic device to its ideal isentropic counterpart. Turbine: actual ÷ ideal work. Compressor/pump: ideal ÷ actual work. Nozzle: actual ÷ ideal exit *kinetic energy*.
equations.note: $h_{2s}$ is the exit enthalpy of the *ideal* (isentropic, $s_2 = s_1$) process to the same exit pressure. For the nozzle, actual exit velocity $V_{2a} = \sqrt{\eta_N}\,V_{2s}$, and the fluid leaves a bit hotter/slower than ideal because of friction.

equations.name: Reversible steady-flow work
equations.useWhen: The maximum work a steady-flow device can produce (or the minimum it needs) between two states. The work scales with $\int v\,dP$, so keep $v$ small during compression, large during expansion.
equations.note: Contrast with closed-system boundary work $\int P\,dv$. For a liquid, $v$ barely changes, giving the compact pump relation $w = v\,\Delta P$ — no property tables needed.

equations.name: Reversible compressor work (ideal gas)
equations.useWhen: Sizing the reversible work to compress an ideal gas from $P_1$ to $P_2$. Compare the three paths: **isentropic** ($Pv^k$) costs the most, **isothermal** ($Pv$) the least, **polytropic** ($Pv^n$, $1<n<k$) sits between.
equations.note: Isothermal needs the least work because cooling keeps $v$ small — the motivation for intercooling. Temperatures absolute; $R$ in kJ/(kg·K).

equations.name: Multistage compression with intercooling
equations.useWhen: Minimizing the work to compress a gas over a large pressure ratio. Split it into stages with cooling back to $T_1$ between them; total work is least when the **pressure ratio is equal across every stage**.
equations.note: For two stages the optimum intermediate pressure is the geometric mean $P_x = \sqrt{P_1 P_2}$, and the two stages then do identical work. Cooling between stages shrinks $v$ in the second stage, cutting its $\int v\,dP$.

equations.name: Entropy balance
rearrangements: \dot S_{gen} = \sum \dot m_{out} s_{out} - \sum \dot m_{in} s_{in} - \sum \frac{\dot Q_k}{T_k}
equations.useWhen: Finding entropy generation in any closed or open system — the second-law analog of the energy balance.
equations.note: Entropy enters/leaves with heat ($Q/T$) and with mass ($\dot m s$), and is *generated* internally by irreversibility.

glossary.definition: A property defined by $dS = (\delta Q/T)_{int,rev}$, measuring disorder / the unavailability of energy for work. Units kJ/K (specific: kJ/(kg·K)).
$\oint \delta Q/T \le 0$ for any cycle; the basis for defining entropy as a property.
Entropy created by irreversibilities within a system; $\ge 0$ always, $= 0$ only for reversible processes.
The total entropy of an isolated system (or system + surroundings) can never decrease: $S_{gen} \ge 0$.
$T\,ds = du + P\,dv$ and $T\,ds = dh - v\,dP$; relate entropy to other properties and generate the working $\Delta s$ formulas.
A reversible + adiabatic process, for which $\Delta s = 0$ ($s_2 = s_1$). The ideal model for turbines, pumps, nozzles, compressors.
$k = c_p/c_v$; appears in the isentropic ideal-gas relations.
Ratio comparing a real adiabatic device to its isentropic ideal — actual/ideal work for a turbine, ideal/actual for a compressor.
$S_{in} - S_{out} + S_{gen} = \Delta S_{system}$; the second-law bookkeeping equation, used to find $S_{gen}$.
Heat carries entropy $Q/T$ across a boundary; work carries none. Mass flow carries $\dot m s$.
For an ideal gas with constant specific heats: $T_2/T_1 = (P_2/P_1)^{(k-1)/k} = (v_1/v_2)^{k-1}$ and $Pv^k = $ const.

$s^\circ(T) = \int_0^T c_p\,dT/T$, the temperature-dependent part of an ideal gas's entropy, tabulated (Table A-17). Used in the exact $\Delta s = s_2^\circ - s_1^\circ - R\ln(P_2/P_1)$ for large $\Delta T$.
Accounting for $c_p(T)$ varying with temperature via the tabulated $s^\circ$ (and $P_r$, $v_r$), instead of assuming constant $c_p$. Needed when $\Delta T$ is large.
A dimensionless, temperature-only function tabulated for air; for an isentropic process $(P_2/P_1)_s = P_{r2}/P_{r1}$. Lets you find $T_2$ accurately without assuming constant $k$.
A dimensionless, temperature-only function tabulated for air; for an isentropic process $(v_2/v_1)_s = v_{r2}/v_{r1}$. The natural tool for volume-ratio (engine compression-ratio) problems.
$w_{rev} = -\int v\,dP - \Delta ke - \Delta pe$; for a liquid ($v$ const) it becomes $w = v\,\Delta P$. Depends on $v\,dP$, unlike closed-system $P\,dv$.

Splitting a compression into stages with cooling back to $T_1$ between them to approach the low-work isothermal limit. Work is minimized when each stage has the same pressure ratio; two-stage optimum is $P_x = \sqrt{P_1 P_2}$.
Actual exit kinetic energy ÷ ideal (isentropic) exit KE at the same exit pressure: $\eta_N = V_{2a}^2/V_{2s}^2 = (h_1 - h_{2a})/(h_1 - h_{2s})$.

tips: **Two ideal-gas $\Delta s$ forms — match them to your data.** Given $T$ and $v$? Use $c_v\ln(T_2/T_1) + R\ln(v_2/v_1)$. Given $T$ and $P$? Use $c_p\ln(T_2/T_1) - R\ln(P_2/P_1)$.
**Isentropic = reversible AND adiabatic → $s_2 = s_1$.** Set entropy equal at inlet and outlet to find the ideal exit state, *then* apply isentropic efficiency for the real device.

**$h_{2s}$ vs $h_2$.** $h_{2s}$ is the ideal (isentropic) exit enthalpy at the actual exit pressure; $h_2$ is the real one. Turbine efficiency = actual drop $(h_1-h_2)$ over ideal drop $(h_1-h_{2s})$.
**Entropy is generated, not conserved.** Unlike energy, $S_{gen} > 0$ for real processes. A computed $S_{gen} < 0$ means an error or an impossible process.
**All logs take absolute temperatures (K).** Every $\ln(T_2/T_1)$ uses kelvin; a ratio of °C values is wrong.
**Don't confuse adiabatic with isentropic.** Adiabatic ($Q=0$) is isentropic only if it is *also* reversible. A throttling valve is adiabatic but generates entropy.

**Big ΔT ⇒ drop constant specific heats.** For large temperature swings the constant-$c_p$ formulas lose accuracy — switch to the $s^\circ$ table method: $\Delta s = s_2^\circ - s_1^\circ - R\ln(P_2/P_1)$. Monatomic gases (He, Ar) are the exception — their $c_p$ is truly constant.

**$P_r$/$v_r$ recipe for isentropic states:** read $P_{r1}$ (or $v_{r1}$) at $T_1$, multiply by the pressure ratio $P_2/P_1$ (or volume ratio $v_2/v_1$), then read $T_2$ back off the table at the new value. Use $v_r$ when you're given a volume/compression ratio, $P_r$ when given pressures.

**Steady-flow work uses $\int v\,dP$, not $\int P\,dv$.** The closed-system boundary-work integral and the steady-flow one look alike but aren't — mixing them up is a classic error. For a liquid, $w = v\,\Delta P$ (no tables needed).

**To cut compressor work, cut the specific volume.** Isothermal compression costs the least, isentropic the most; multistage compression with intercooling approaches the isothermal limit. For two stages, split at $P_x = \sqrt{P_1 P_2}$ so both stages have equal pressure ratio and equal work.
